items.title: Temporal Panel Selection in Ongoing Citizens' Assemblies
items.authors: Yusuf Hakan Kalayci and Evi Micha
items.summary: The paper formalizes representation over a sequence of rotating panels and presents algorithms with different fairness and proportionality guarantees. It extends a one-time selection question into an ongoing institutional design problem. The guarantees hold within a mathematical model; this is not an experiment showing that rotating assemblies improve real-world policy.
items.headline: Selection algorithms consider representation across successive citizen panels

evidence.question: How can rotating panels represent people fairly over time?
evidence.method: Formal model and algorithmic analysis of temporal selection.
evidence.limitations: Guarantees depend on the modeled population and fairness definitions; governance outcomes are not tested.

explainer.finding: The paper develops ways to balance representation and participation chances across successive citizen panels.
explainer.method: It defines a formal selection problem and proves properties of algorithms under particular fairness and proportionality definitions.
explainer.meaning: A fair-looking panel today can still repeatedly exclude some people over time. Rotating membership makes the sequence of selections part of the design problem.
explainer.limits: Mathematical guarantees depend on the model. The paper does not test whether rotating panels improve policy, deliberation, or public trust.

items.title: Communicating Program Eligibility: A Supplemental Security Income (SSI) Field Experiment
items.authors: Jeffrey Hemmeter, John Phillips, Elana Safran, Nicholas Wilson
items.summary: A randomized direct-mail experiment covering more than four million older individuals tested messages about likely program eligibility. Letters increased take-up, and some behavioral wording improved their effects, but application rates remained no greater than 7% over the full follow-up. Information is one administrative barrier, not a complete explanation of participation; application growth also involved trade-offs in award likelihood and amounts.
items.headline: Eligibility letters increase benefit take-up but leave substantial barriers

evidence.question: Can clearer eligibility communication improve access to a public program?
evidence.method: Randomized field experiment comparing mail interventions, with administrative follow-up.
evidence.limitations: Specific population and program; applications, awards, and broader welfare effects are distinct outcomes.

explainer.finding: Letters about likely benefit eligibility increased participation, while applications remained limited over follow-up.
explainer.method: A randomized mailing experiment covered more than four million older individuals and compared message designs using administrative outcomes.
explainer.meaning: Telling someone a service exists can remove an information barrier without removing the documents, time, or practical effort needed to obtain it.
explainer.limits: Applications, awards, and wider welfare outcomes are different measures. The results belong to this program and population; clearer communication is not a complete participation solution.

items.title: Financial Spillover Effects from Electronic Government Transfers: Evidence from an At-Scale Experiment in Indonesia
items.authors: Abhijit Banerjee, Rema Hanna, Benjamin A. Olken, Elan Satriawan, Sudarno Sumarto
items.summary: Using a randomized district rollout in Indonesia, the study examines whether banking agents established for electronic benefit distribution also increase household use of other financial services. It finds no detectable effect on those other services, alongside a small increase in neighborhood shops. The result separates successful transfer delivery from an assumed broader financial-inclusion effect; it does not establish that digital delivery has no benefits.
items.headline: Electronic benefit delivery does not automatically expand other financial services

evidence.question: Do delivery reforms create financial-service spillovers beyond their primary purpose?
evidence.method: Analysis of an at-scale randomized district rollout in Indonesia.
evidence.limitations: No detectable effect is not proof of an exact zero; results belong to the studied outcomes, setting, and period.

explainer.finding: The study found no detectable increase in household use of other financial services from the tested electronic-transfer rollout.
explainer.method: The analysis used randomized rollout across Indonesian districts to assess spillovers beyond the benefit-delivery function.
explainer.meaning: A channel that successfully delivers a payment need not also change how people save or borrow. The hoped-for side effect needs its own evidence.
explainer.limits: No detectable effect is not proof of an exact zero. The result does not imply that digital delivery lacks benefits; it concerns the measured spillover outcomes.

items.title: A large-scale field experiment on participatory decision-making in China
items.authors: Sherry Jueyu Wu, Ke Michael Mai, Ming Zhuang, Fangxin Yi
items.summary: Communities were randomly assigned invitations to deliberate and allocate local budgets. Six months later, the study found increased civic engagement beyond budgeting, alongside changes in evaluations of government and society. The intervention offers evidence about participation in one institutional setting. It does not show that consultation and binding decision authority are equivalent, or establish the same effects in other political systems.
items.headline: Community budgeting participation changes civic engagement in a field experiment

evidence.question: Does participation in community budgeting affect wider civic engagement?
evidence.method: Community-level randomized field intervention with follow-up outcome measurement.
evidence.limitations: Setting-specific intervention and follow-up; reported attitudes and observed institutional change are different measures.

explainer.finding: Participation in a local budgeting intervention was followed by higher civic engagement beyond budgeting in the study’s follow-up.
explainer.method: Communities were randomly assigned invitations to deliberate and allocate local budgets, with outcomes measured six months later.
explainer.meaning: A concrete opportunity to make a local decision may affect engagement beyond that single meeting. A field comparison tests that possibility in an actual setting.
explainer.limits: The result is setting-specific. Attitudes, engagement, binding authority, and policy implementation are distinct outcomes, and effects need not transfer unchanged to other systems.

items.title: Civil Service Adoption in America: The Political Influence of City Employees
items.authors: Sarah F. Anzia and Jessica Trounstine
items.venue: American Political Science Review; online 2024, issue 2025
items.summary: The authors combine historical municipal data and qualitative evidence to investigate how public employees helped advance civil-service rules. Organized firefighters and other employees appear as participants in institutional change, rather than merely its beneficiaries. The observational historical design supports a mechanism to examine; it does not isolate all competing causes or establish that every civil-service arrangement has the same effects.
items.headline: Historical evidence links employee organization to civil-service adoption

evidence.question: Which groups helped bring about municipal civil-service rules?
evidence.method: Historical quantitative comparison and qualitative evidence from American cities.
evidence.limitations: Observational evidence and historical measurement limits; adoption and later performance are separate questions.

explainer.finding: Historical evidence identifies organized public employees as contributors to the adoption of municipal civil-service rules.
explainer.method: The authors combine quantitative comparisons of American cities with qualitative historical evidence about institutional change.
explainer.meaning: People affected by employment rules can also organize to shape those rules. That changes a story in which employees appear only as passive beneficiaries.
explainer.limits: The design is observational and historical. It does not eliminate every alternative cause or show that all civil-service systems have identical consequences.

items.title: Fair algorithms for selecting citizens’ assemblies
items.authors: Bailey Flanigan, Paul Gölz, Anupam Gupta, Brett Hennig, Ariel D. Procaccia
items.summary: The study develops algorithms balancing representative panels with more equal individual selection probabilities, and evaluates them on real assembly datasets. It is useful background for newer work on rotating assemblies. Fairness within a volunteer pool does not solve recruitment bias, agenda-setting, or implementation of recommendations; those remain distinct institutional choices.
items.headline: Fair selection requires more than drawing volunteers one at a time

evidence.question: How can panel selection balance quotas and individual chances fairly?
evidence.method: Formal algorithmic guarantees and evaluation on ten real assembly datasets.
evidence.limitations: Model-defined fairness within recruitment pools; no causal test of policy quality or population-wide participation.

explainer.finding: Algorithms can balance representative panel requirements with more equal individual selection chances within a recruitment pool.
explainer.method: The paper provides formal guarantees and evaluates its algorithms using ten real citizens’ assembly datasets.
explainer.meaning: Drawing one volunteer at a time can leave later choices constrained by quotas. Considering complete possible panels changes how fairly chances can be allocated.
explainer.limits: Fairness among volunteers does not fix who volunteered, who sets the agenda, or whether recommendations are implemented. Those require additional institutional choices and evidence.

items.title: Dead Ends and Policy Change in Chinese Experimental Governance
items.headline: Following stalled initiatives reveals what success stories miss
items.summary: Most sampled Chinese policy explorations lost documentary follow-up. This indicates possible interruption, not a measured failure rate.

evidence.question: What happens to early policy initiatives?
evidence.method: Text matching tracked 27,103 explorations announced in 2013–2018, comparing continued coverage with disappearance; two cases added context.
evidence.limitations: Observational document proxies, not causal identification.

explainer.finding: Only 11.7% retained documentary coverage six years after announcement.
explainer.method: A year without mentions signaled possible interruption; comparisons examined administrative level, central recognition, and leadership changes.
explainer.meaning: A mobile-payment initiative can disappear while the broader payment system grows. Following the specific instrument distinguishes abandonment from changes in goals.
explainer.limits: Missing documents, changed wording, and completed initiatives can affect classification. Early explorations do not represent all implemented policies; disappearance does not prove ineffectiveness.

editorialReview.reason: Teaches policy follow-through and measurement limits; methods, results, cases, and caveats read.

items.title: Three Configurations of In-House Government Consulting: Public-Value Purpose and Organizational Viability
items.headline: Government advisory teams need measures that fit their purpose
items.summary: Eight documentary cases suggest three ways to organize internal government advice. These are proposed designs, not proven improvements in cost or performance.

evidence.question: How should governments organize internal advisory capacity?
evidence.method: Theory development using public documents about eight units in five countries.
evidence.limitations: Nonrepresentative cases; no causal performance evaluation.

explainer.finding: The framework separates teams handling sensitive reforms, teams reusing solutions, and teams assembling dispersed expertise.
explainer.method: Safford compared public records, checking official accounts against independent scrutiny where available.
explainer.meaning: For example, judging an emergency reform team only by billable hours could encourage routine assignments that displace its purpose.
explainer.limits: Cases were deliberately selected; evidence quality varies. No causal test established which design works best.

editorialReview.reason: Read methods, case comparisons, and conclusion; useful institutional-design framework.

items.title: Imperial Aid and Tax Mobilization in Late Colonial Africa
items.headline: Aid and tax collection: why administrators mattered
items.summary: In 12 British African colonies, aid was more strongly associated with tax collection under career governors. Higher revenue does not establish improved welfare.

evidence.question: When did development aid encourage local taxation?
evidence.method: Archival grant records, annual tax regressions, and an instrumental-variable analysis using British financial shocks interacting with aid commitments.
evidence.limitations: The instrument assumes shocks affect taxes through aid; governor selection was not random.

explainer.finding: Aid–tax relationships differed with governors' recruitment and career backgrounds.
explainer.method: The researcher compared administrations and used disbursement fluctuations to investigate causation; the instrumental estimate met a 90%, not 95%, significance threshold.
explainer.meaning: For example, a project requiring local cofunding gives administrators a reason to collect taxes—if their incentives support that requirement.
explainer.limits: This colonial setting does not establish that similar arrangements improve welfare or work in today's aid programmes.

editorialReview.reason: Read archival design, regression results, identification assumptions, recruitment comparisons, and conclusion. Teaches administrative incentives with explicit causal limits.

items.title: Democratic Accountability with Citizen Coproduction
items.headline: Who gets the blame when public services need everyone’s help?
items.authors: Jie Ma, Keith E. Schnakenberg and Ian R. Turner
items.summary: A mathematical model shows how citizen participation changes what policy failure reveals about an official’s competence. Under some conditions, stronger participation can discourage reform. These are theoretical predictions, not measured effects.

evidence.question: How does voluntary citizen participation affect accountability and reform incentives?
evidence.method: Solved a sequential game of policy choice, citizen cooperation and voting using Bayesian updating.
evidence.limitations: Assumes shared desired outcomes, observed participation and a contest against one challenger.

explainer.finding: Low participation makes failure less revealing. Officials who could lose after failure may therefore avoid reforms when participation rises.
explainer.method: Derived equilibrium conditions and compared incentives across participation costs and electoral positions; no field experiment was conducted.
explainer.meaning: If a reading programme needs parents’ help, poor results could reflect its design or limited participation. Those explanations carry different implications for evaluating the school board.
explainer.limits: Predictions depend on the model’s assumptions and electoral setting. They do not establish that participation is harmful or describe any particular politician.

editorialReview.reason: Read primary model, equilibrium analysis and scope limits; teaches accountability without campaign commentary.
